title: The Clock That Follows the Moon
bodyMd:
This is an informational passage. Three places are marked with a bracketed number and shown in **bold**. Each question names the place it asks about.

**Paragraph 1.** In a workshop above a hardware store in the town of Harnett, Lucia Okonjo builds clocks that are wrong on purpose. An ordinary clock divides the solar day into twenty-four hours. A tide clock keeps a different day, because the moon, not the sun, does most of the work of lifting the sea. Its single hand travels once around a face marked HIGH at the top and LOW at the bottom, and the trip takes twelve hours and twenty-five minutes.

**Paragraph 2.** **[1] Okonjo learned the trade from her grandfather, a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing fleet, he never built a tide clock himself.** Those extra twenty-five minutes are the whole difficulty. Any movement can be slowed, but a tide movement has to be slowed by exactly the right amount and then hold that error, unchanged, for years.

**Paragraph 3.** **[2] Each of her movements is individually adjusted one at a time by hand.** She files a fraction of a milligram from the balance wheel, runs the movement for a week against a reference clock, and files again. A tide clock that gains ninety seconds a month will be pointing at LOW, by the end of its first summer, while the flats lie under half a metre of water.

**Paragraph 4.** The clocks sell steadily, which still surprises Okonjo, since anyone with a phone can look up a tide table in seconds. Her customers tell her that a table gives them a number and the clock gives them a picture. **[3]** A glance at the single hand shows not only when the next high water is due but how much of the cycle has already run.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph informational passage about Lucia Okonjo, a clockmaker in the invented town of Harnett who builds tide clocks whose single hand completes one circuit in twelve hours and twenty-five minutes. Paragraph one explains why a tide clock keeps lunar rather than solar time. Paragraph two describes how she learned the trade and why the extra twenty-five minutes are difficult to engineer. Paragraph three describes the adjustment process and what goes wrong when a tide clock runs fast. Paragraph four reports that customers buy the clocks even though tide tables are available on a phone. Three places are marked for editing. Marked place one, which opens paragraph two, is the whole sentence: "Okonjo learned the trade from her grandfather, a watchmaker who repaired instruments for the fishing fleet, he never built a tide clock himself." Marked place two, which opens paragraph three, is the whole sentence: "Each of her movements is individually adjusted one at a time by hand." Marked place three is an empty position in paragraph four, between the sentence about a number and a picture and the sentence beginning "A glance at the single hand".

provenance.notes: Original passage. Lucia Okonjo, the town of Harnett and every detail of her workshop are invented for this item set; nothing is taken from, or modelled on, a published ACT English passage.
